Something is intimidating if it makes you feel nervous, small, or unsure of yourself — because it seems too powerful, too difficult, too impressive, or too threatening for you to easily face or handle.

When something intimidates you, your confidence drops. You feel like hesitating, backing away, or doubting whether you're capable enough.
The Two Main Ways Something Can Be Intimidating

1. It feels threatening or dangerous.
A barking dog blocking your path is intimidating. An aggressive person who looks ready to fight is intimidating. This triggers a fear response — you feel unsafe.

2. It feels too impressive, too big, or too far beyond you.
This is the more common, everyday use. A 1,000-page textbook on your first day of study is intimidating. A world-class chess grandmaster sitting across from you is intimidating. You don't feel scared in a dangerous sense — you feel small, inadequate, or out of your depth.

Both types share the same result: they shake your confidence and make you feel hesitant or overwhelmed.
Who or What Can Be Intimidating?

Almost anything:

  • A person: "My new boss has an intimidating personality — she never smiles and always looks serious."
  • A task: "Learning to code felt intimidating at first."
  • A place: "Walking into a grand courtroom for the first time can be intimidating."
  • A situation: "Speaking in front of 500 people is intimidating for most people."
  • A subject: "Quantum physics seems intimidating, but the basics are learnable."
  • A scale or size: "The sheer length of this novel is intimidating."
Intentional vs. Unintentional — A Key Nuance

A person can be intimidating without meaning to be.

A very tall, quiet, serious person may intimidate others simply by their presence — they never intended to. A highly skilled expert can make beginners feel intimidated just by how effortlessly they perform.

But a person can also deliberately try to be intimidating — by staring you down, speaking aggressively, or using their authority to make you feel powerless.

The word "intimidating" can describe both situations. You rely on context to know which is meant.
Is "Intimidating" Always Negative?

Not always — but it almost always signals that someone feels less confident in response to it.

Sometimes it's used with a neutral or even admiring tone:

  • "She has an intimidating level of talent." (You're in awe — humbled, not scared.)
  • "The mountain's intimidating scale drew climbers from around the world."

But in most everyday use, calling something intimidating means it's making someone feel anxious or hesitant — which is a negative experience for that person, even if the thing itself is neutral or good.
It's Partly Subjective

The same thing can be intimidating to one person and perfectly normal to another.

  • A loud, crowded city might be intimidating to someone from a quiet village, but not to a city-dweller.
  • A difficult math problem might be intimidating to a student but exciting to a mathematician.

So "intimidating" describes a relationship between something and a person's response to it — not a fixed quality of the thing itself. The thing doesn't change; it's your perception and confidence level that determines whether it feels intimidating.
Example Sentences

1. "The interview panel was so intimidating that he forgot everything he'd prepared."
  2. "Don't let her intimidating appearance fool you — she's actually very warm."
  3. "The mountain looked intimidating from the base, but the hike wasn't actually that hard."
  4. "Learning a new language can feel intimidating, but it gets easier with time."
  5. "He had an intimidating stare that made people uncomfortable."
  6. "The sheer amount of work ahead of us was intimidating."
  7. "She walked into the room with an intimidating confidence — everyone fell silent."

Notice how in sentence 7, "intimidating confidence" is almost a compliment — it means her confidence was so strong that it made others feel a little unsure of themselves.
Words Closely Related to "Intimidating"

Understanding these will show you exactly where "intimidating" fits among similar words:

Daunting — Makes a task feel too big to even begin. Very close to "intimidating" but used almost exclusively for tasks and challenges, rarely for people. "The project is daunting" = I don't know where to start. "Intimidating" works for both people and tasks; "daunting" mainly for tasks.

Formidable — Inspires fear or deep respect because of power, strength, or ability. Slightly more formal and stronger. A "formidable opponent" is one you genuinely fear facing. Something formidable commands respect almost by right; something intimidating just makes you personally feel small.

Frightening — Causes actual fear. Clearly stronger than "intimidating." A frightening movie makes your heart pound; an intimidating boss just makes you nervous before a meeting.

Overwhelming — So much in quantity or intensity that you can't cope. An overwhelming workload might not be intimidating (it doesn't necessarily shake your confidence) — it's just too much to handle. "Overwhelming" is about quantity and overload; "intimidating" is about confidence and power.

Imposing — Grand and impressive in size or appearance, demanding attention and respect. An imposing building is large, serious, and commands your notice. "Imposing" is more about the visual presence of something; "intimidating" is about the emotional effect it has on you.

Threatening — Signals that something could cause you harm. More directly about danger than "intimidating." All threatening things are intimidating, but not all intimidating things are threatening — a genius professor is intimidating but not threatening.
The Opposite of "Intimidating"

Depending on context, the opposite might be:

  • Approachable (for a person — easy to talk to, not scary)
  • Welcoming (for a place or person)
  • Manageable (for a task — feels doable, within reach)
  • Reassuring (for a situation — makes you feel calm and capable)
  • Encouraging (for feedback or an environment)
The Word Family

Since you'll encounter these related forms:

  • To intimidate (verb) = to deliberately make someone feel afraid or unsure, usually to control them or gain power over them. "He tried to intimidate the witness into staying silent."
  • Intimidating (adjective) = describes something that has the quality of causing this feeling. This is what you asked about.
  • Intimidated (adjective) = describes the person who is on the receiving end of this feeling. "She felt intimidated by the crowd." Note: you describe a thing as intimidating, but a person as intimidated.
  • Intimidation (noun) = the act or the experience itself. "The defendant claimed it was an act of intimidation."

A simple test to remember which to use: if you're describing the source of the feeling, use "intimidating." If you're describing the person experiencing the feeling, use "intimidated."

"The exam was intimidating." (The exam is the source.)
"I felt intimidated by the exam." (You are the one experiencing it.)
The Complete Picture

To summarize everything cleanly:

Something is intimidating when it makes you feel nervous, small, hesitant, or out of your depth — whether because it's powerful, difficult, impressive, or threatening. It doesn't have to be dangerous to be intimidating; it just has to make you feel like you might not be enough to handle it. The word applies to people, tasks, places, situations, and ideas. Whether something feels intimidating is partly personal — it depends on who you are and what you're used to. And the thing causing the feeling may or may not be doing so intentionally.
